1 Feature Matching

Core Idea

Feature matching is the process of finding corresponding points, patches, edges, or regions between two or more images of the same scene taken from different positions, at different times, or under different conditions.

This is the foundation for many important computer vision tasks:

  • Fundamental Matrix Estimation: Given two cameras looking at the same scene, the fundamental matrix encodes the geometric relationship between them. We need matched point pairs to compute it.
  • Structure from Motion (SfM): Reconstruct 3D structure of a scene by tracking features across many 2D images taken from different viewpoints.
  • Image Stitching / Panoramas: Align multiple overlapping images by matching features in the overlap regions.
  • Object Recognition: Match feature descriptors from a query image against a database of known objects.

The Matching Pipeline

Feature matching generally follows this pipeline:

1
Detect interest points / keypoints in each image independently
2
Describe each keypoint with a local descriptor (a compact representation of the surrounding patch)
3
Match descriptors between images using distance metrics (Euclidean, Hamming, etc.)
4
Filter false matches using geometric constraints (e.g., RANSAC with epipolar geometry)

2 Interest Points

Definition

An interest point (also called a keypoint or feature point) is a point in an image that has a well-defined, distinctive local neighbourhood — meaning it can be reliably detected and matched even after the image has been transformed (rotated, scaled, etc.).

Why Do We Need Interest Points?

  • Tracking: Which points should we follow as the camera moves? Flat, textureless regions are impossible to track — they look the same after displacement. We need points that are unique and localised.
  • Recognition: Find patches in an image that are likely to tell us something discriminative about the object category.
  • 3D Reconstruction: Find exact correspondences between the same physical point seen from different camera positions.

What Makes a Good Feature?

The key question is: which points can be reliably remembered and re-found after the image is deformed?

  • A flat region has no distinguishing structure — every patch looks the same as its neighbours. Not usable.
  • An edge is distinctive in the perpendicular direction but ambiguous along the edge direction. Partially usable.
  • A corner is distinctive in ALL directions — shifting the window even slightly in any direction gives a very different appearance. Ideal!

Invariant Local Features

The ideal feature detector produces features that are invariant (or at least robust) to:

  • Translation — the camera moves laterally
  • Rotation — the camera or object rotates
  • Scale change — the camera zooms in or out
  • Illumination change — different lighting conditions
  • Affine distortion — viewpoint change

Keypoint Matching in Action

3 Interest Point Detection

The Sliding Window Intuition

The key insight behind most corner/interest-point detectors: place a small window around a candidate pixel and ask what happens to pixel intensities if you shift that window slightly.

  • (a) Flat region: Shifting the window in any direction produces no change in intensity. We cannot tell where the window was → not an interest point.
  • (b) Edge: Shifting along the edge direction produces no change (the edge looks the same). Shifting perpendicular to the edge gives a large change. We can only localise in one direction → poor interest point.
  • (c) Corner: Shifting in ANY direction produces a large intensity change. We can precisely localise the point in both x and y → excellent interest point!

Properties of a Good Interest Point Detector

  • 🎯 High recall: Detect all (or most) true interest points
  • ✅ High precision: No (or few) false interest points
  • 📍 Good localisation: Detected position is close to the true position
  • 🔇 Noise robustness: Reliable under noisy conditions
  • ⚡ Efficiency: Fast enough for practical use

Corner Detection Approaches

There are two main families:

  • Intensity-based (gradient methods): Analyse the image derivatives / gradient structure directly. Harris detector falls here. Faster and more commonly used.
  • Boundary-based: First extract edges, then analyse the curvature of those edge curves. High curvature points are corners. More complex, rarely used in practice.

The Aperture Problem

What is the Aperture Problem?

When you observe an image through a small aperture (window), you can only see the component of motion perpendicular to a visible edge. The motion along the edge is invisible — there are infinitely many motions consistent with what you observe. This is the aperture problem.

At a corner, two or more edges meet at different orientations. This breaks the ambiguity — there is now only ONE consistent motion. This is why corners are ideal for tracking and matching.

4 Harris Interest Point Detector

The Harris detector (Harris & Stephens, 1988) formalises the sliding-window intuition into a mathematically rigorous framework. It is one of the most widely used and studied corner detectors ever developed.

4.1 Correlation, Auto-correlation & SSD

Before deriving the Harris detector, we need to understand three related measures:

Cross-Correlation (how similar image patch f is to template h at position i,j):
(f ⊗ h)(i, j) = Σk,l f(k, l) · h(i+k, j+l)

Auto-Correlation (how similar a patch is to a shifted version of itself):
(f ⊗ f)(i, j) = Σk,l f(k, l) · f(i+k, j+l)

Sum of Squared Differences (SSD) (how different two patches are):
SSD(i, j) = Σk,l [f(k, l) − h(i+k, j+l)]²
Cross-correlation measures similarity. Auto-correlation compares the image against a shifted copy of itself. SSD measures dissimilarity (lower = more similar). SSD and cross-correlation are related: SSD = ||f||² + ||h||² − 2(f ⊗ h), so maximising cross-correlation ≈ minimising SSD.

4.2 The Harris Error Function E(u, v)

E(u, v) = Σx,y w(x, y) · [I(x+u, y+v) − I(x, y)]²
E(u,v) measures the total intensity change when the image window is shifted by (u,v).
• w(x,y) is a window weighting function — either a rectangular box window or a Gaussian (preferred, gives smooth response and down-weights pixels at the window edges).
• I(x,y) is the image intensity at pixel (x,y).
• We want E(u,v) to be LARGE for small (u,v) at corner locations.
💡
Intuition: If E(u,v) is large even for tiny shifts (u,v) in all directions, the patch is a corner. If E is only large in one direction, it's an edge. If E stays near zero regardless of shift, it's a flat region.

Taylor Expansion Approximation

Computing E(u,v) for every possible shift is expensive. Instead, we use a first-order Taylor expansion of I(x+u, y+v) around (x,y):

I(x+u, y+v) ≈ I(x,y) + u·Ix + v·Iy

So: I(x+u, y+v) − I(x,y) ≈ u·Ix + v·Iy

Substituting into E:
E(u,v) ≈ Σx,y w(x,y) · (u·Ix + v·Iy)²
Ix = ∂I/∂x and Iy = ∂I/∂y are the image gradient components (computed using Sobel or similar filters). This approximation converts E from an expensive pixel-comparison into a simple quadratic form.

4.3 The Structure Matrix M (Second Moment Matrix)

Expanding the squared term and writing it in matrix form:

E(u, v) ≈ [u, v] · M · [u, v]ᵀ

where the Structure Matrix (or Second Moment Matrix) M is:

M = Σx,y w(x,y) · Ix²    IxIy
IxIy    Iy² = Σ ∇I · (∇I)ᵀ
• M is a 2×2 symmetric positive semi-definite matrix.
• Each entry is the windowed sum of gradient products: Σw·Ix², Σw·IxIy, Σw·Iy².
• The expression Σ∇I·(∇I)ᵀ makes it clear: M is the sum of outer products of gradient vectors — it captures the "spread" of gradient directions in the window.
• Gaussian w(x,y) is preferred over a box filter as it gives a smooth, isotropic response.

E(u,v) as an Ellipse

The expression E(u,v) = [u,v] M [u,v]ᵀ is the equation of an ellipse in (u,v) space. The shape of this ellipse tells us about the local image structure:

  • A round ellipse (nearly circular) → intensity changes equally in all directions → corner
  • A very elongated ellipse → intensity changes mainly in one direction → edge
  • A very large ellipse (barely changes) → flat region
M can be diagonalised (since it's symmetric) as:

M = R · λ₁   0
0   λ₂ · Rᵀ

where λ₁, λ₂ are the eigenvalues of M, and R is the rotation matrix of eigenvectors.
The eigenvalues give the magnitude of intensity change along the two principal (eigen) directions.
The eigenvectors of M point along the directions of maximum and minimum intensity change. The eigenvalues measure the rate of change in those directions.

4.4 Eigenvalue Classification of Pixels

🏔 Flat Region
λ₁ ≈ 0, λ₂ ≈ 0
Both eigenvalues are small. Intensity is nearly constant in ALL directions. The window looks the same wherever you move it.
📏 Edge
λ₁ ≫ λ₂ ≈ 0 (or vice versa)
One eigenvalue is large (across the edge), the other is small (along the edge). Intensity changes only in one direction.
🔵 Corner
λ₁ large, λ₂ large
BOTH eigenvalues are large. Intensity changes significantly in ALL directions. This is our ideal interest point!
🔑
Physical meaning of eigenvalues: λ₁ and λ₂ are the curvatures of the error function E(u,v) in the two principal directions. A large eigenvalue means E grows steeply in that direction — the patch is very distinctive there.

4.5 The Harris Corner Response Score R

Problem with direct eigenvalue comparison: Computing eigenvalues is expensive (requires solving a characteristic equation). Harris avoids this entirely by using cheaper matrix invariants.

Harris Corner Response Score:

R = det(M) − k · [trace(M)]²

Expanded:
R = λ₁λ₂ − k(λ₁ + λ₂)²

where:
det(M) = Ix²·Iy² − (IxIy)² = λ₁λ₂
trace(M) = Ix² + Iy² = λ₁ + λ₂
k ∈ [0.04, 0.06] (empirical sensitivity constant)
Key: det(M) and trace(M) can be computed DIRECTLY from Ix², Iy², IxIy — no eigenvalue decomposition needed!
• det(M) is large when BOTH eigenvalues are large (corner condition)
• trace(M) is large when AT LEAST ONE eigenvalue is large
• k penalises the trace, so the score is only large when BOTH λ values are large (true corners)

Interpreting R:

  • 🟢 R is large and positive (R > threshold): Both eigenvalues large → CORNER / interest point
  • 🔴 R is negative with large magnitude: One eigenvalue much larger than the other → EDGE
  • ⚪ |R| is small: Both eigenvalues small → FLAT REGION

4.6 Harris Detector — Full Algorithm

Harris Corner Detector Algorithm
1
Compute Gradients
Calculate Ix = ∂I/∂x and Iy = ∂I/∂y using Sobel filters
2
Compute Gradient Products
At each pixel, compute Ix², Iy², and IxIy (these are the entries of M)
3
Gaussian Windowing
Convolve Ix², Iy², IxIy with a Gaussian kernel (this computes the weighted sum Σw(x,y)·(·) that defines M)
4
Compute Corner Response R
R = det(M) − k·[trace(M)]² = (Ix²·Iy² − (IxIy)²) − k·(Ix²+Iy²)²
5
Threshold & Suppress
Find pixels where R > threshold, then apply non-maximum suppression to keep only local maxima

5 Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues

Definition

Given a square matrix A, a non-zero vector x is called an eigenvector of A if multiplying A by x gives back x scaled by a scalar — i.e., the direction of x is unchanged by the transformation A.

Eigenvalue Equation:

A · x = λ · x

which rearranges to:
(A − λI) · x = 0

For a non-trivial solution, we need:
det(A − λI) = 0 ← the characteristic equation
λ (lambda) = eigenvalue — a scalar that tells you HOW MUCH the eigenvector is scaled. x = eigenvector — the special direction in which A acts purely as a scaling (not a rotation). For a 2×2 matrix, the characteristic equation is a quadratic giving two eigenvalues λ₁, λ₂.

Worked Example with a 2×2 Matrix

Let A = 2   1
1   2

Characteristic equation: det(A − λI) = (2−λ)(2−λ) − 1·1 = λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0

Roots: λ₁ = 3, λ₂ = 1

For λ₁ = 3: (A − 3I)x = 0 → -1   1
1   -1x = 0 → x₁ = [1, 1]ᵀ / √2

For λ₂ = 1: (A − I)x = 0 → x₂ = [1, −1]ᵀ / √2
The two eigenvectors are perpendicular (orthogonal) — always true for symmetric matrices like M in Harris.

Why This Matters for Harris

The structure matrix M is a 2×2 symmetric positive semi-definite matrix. Its two eigenvectors point along the directions of maximum and minimum intensity change in the image window. The corresponding eigenvalues λ₁ and λ₂ tell us the magnitude of intensity change in those directions.

  • If λ₁ ≫ λ₂ → only one direction of strong change → edge
  • If λ₁ ≈ λ₂ ≫ 0 → both directions are equally strong → corner/blob
  • If λ₁ ≈ λ₂ ≈ 0 → no strong changes in any direction → flat region

Key Properties of M's Eigenvalues

  • Real: M is symmetric, so all eigenvalues are real numbers
  • Non-negative: M is positive semi-definite, so λ₁, λ₂ ≥ 0
  • Orthogonal eigenvectors: The two eigenvectors are always perpendicular
  • det(M) = λ₁ · λ₂ and trace(M) = λ₁ + λ₂ — these let Harris avoid explicit eigenvalue computation

Section A — Correlation, Auto-correlation, SSD

import numpy as np
import cv2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
from scipy.signal import convolve2d

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# A. CORRELATION, AUTO-CORRELATION, AND SSD
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def cross_correlation(f, h):
    """
    Cross-correlation: how similar is template h to image f at each position?
    (f ⊗ h)(i,j) = Σ_kl  f(k,l) * h(i+k, j+l)
    
    In practice, cross-correlation = convolution with h flipped 180°.
    scipy / OpenCV implement this directly.
    """
    # Flip h to convert correlation to convolution
    h_flipped = h[::-1, ::-1]
    return convolve2d(f, h_flipped, mode='same', boundary='symm')


def auto_correlation(f, window_size=5):
    """
    Auto-correlation: compares patch to a shifted version of itself.
    (f ⊗ f)(i,j) = Σ_kl  f(k,l) * f(i+k, j+l)
    
    Returns the auto-correlation at each pixel location.
    """
    f_flipped = f[::-1, ::-1]
    return convolve2d(f, f_flipped, mode='same', boundary='symm')


def ssd(patch1, patch2):
    """
    Sum of Squared Differences between two patches.
    SSD = Σ (f(k,l) - h(i+k, j+l))²
    Returns 0 for identical patches; larger = more different.
    """
    return np.sum((patch1.astype(np.float32) - patch2.astype(np.float32))**2)


def template_matching_ssd(image, template):
    """
    Slide template over image, compute SSD at each position.
    Minimum SSD = best match location.
    """
    h, w = template.shape
    H, W = image.shape
    result = np.zeros((H - h + 1, W - w + 1))

    for i in range(H - h + 1):
        for j in range(W - w + 1):
            patch = image[i:i+h, j:j+w]
            result[i, j] = ssd(patch, template)

    # Best match at minimum SSD
    best_loc = np.unravel_index(result.argmin(), result.shape)
    return result, best_loc

Section B — Structure Matrix M and Corner Response R 

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# B. HARRIS ERROR FUNCTION E(u,v) AND STRUCTURE MATRIX M
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def compute_structure_matrix(img, sigma_grad=1.0, sigma_window=1.5):
    """
    Compute the Harris Structure Matrix M at every pixel.
    
    M = Σ w(x,y) * [[Ix², IxIy], [IxIy, Iy²]]
      = [[Σ w*Ix²,   Σ w*IxIy],
         [Σ w*IxIy,  Σ w*Iy² ]]
    
    Parameters:
        img          : float grayscale image [0,1]
        sigma_grad   : σ for gradient computation (image smoothing before derivatives)
        sigma_window : σ for the Gaussian window function w(x,y)
    Returns:
        M11, M12, M22 : the three unique entries of M at each pixel
        Ix, Iy        : gradient images
    """
    # Step 1: Smooth the image slightly before computing gradients
    img_smooth = gaussian_filter(img, sigma=sigma_grad)

    # Step 2: Compute image gradients Ix and Iy using Sobel kernels
    Kx = np.array([[-1, 0, 1],
                   [-2, 0, 2],
                   [-1, 0, 1]], dtype=np.float32)
    Ky = Kx.T   # Sobel in y = transposed Sobel in x

    Ix = convolve2d(img_smooth, Kx, mode='same', boundary='symm')
    Iy = convolve2d(img_smooth, Ky, mode='same', boundary='symm')

    # Step 3: Compute the three entries of M (gradient products)
    Ix2  = Ix * Ix   # Ix²  → M[0,0]
    Iy2  = Iy * Iy   # Iy²  → M[1,1]
    IxIy = Ix * Iy   # IxIy → M[0,1] = M[1,0]

    # Step 4: Apply Gaussian window w(x,y) to each entry
    #         This computes Σ w(x,y)*Ix² etc. over the neighbourhood
    M11 = gaussian_filter(Ix2,  sigma=sigma_window)  # Σ w·Ix²
    M22 = gaussian_filter(Iy2,  sigma=sigma_window)  # Σ w·Iy²
    M12 = gaussian_filter(IxIy, sigma=sigma_window)  # Σ w·IxIy

    return M11, M12, M22, Ix, Iy


def harris_response(M11, M12, M22, k=0.05):
    """
    Compute the Harris corner response R at every pixel.
    
    R = det(M) - k * trace(M)²
      = (M11*M22 - M12²) - k*(M11 + M22)²
      = λ₁λ₂ - k(λ₁+λ₂)²
    
    R > 0   (large) → CORNER
    R < 0   (large magnitude) → EDGE
    |R| ≈ 0         → FLAT REGION
    
    k is empirically chosen in range [0.04, 0.06].
    """
    det_M   = M11 * M22 - M12**2     # det(M) = λ₁λ₂
    trace_M = M11 + M22               # trace(M) = λ₁+λ₂
    R       = det_M - k * trace_M**2  # Harris score
    return R

Section C — Non-Maximum Suppression for Corner Points 

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# C. NON-MAXIMUM SUPPRESSION AND KEYPOINT EXTRACTION
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def non_max_suppression_corners(R, window_size=5):
    """
    Suppress any corner response pixel that is not a local maximum
    within a (window_size × window_size) neighbourhood.
    
    Returns a binary mask: True at local maxima positions.
    """
    from scipy.ndimage import maximum_filter
    
    # Find local maxima using a max-filter
    local_max = maximum_filter(R, size=window_size)
    
    # A pixel is a local maximum if its R equals the max in its window
    is_max = (R == local_max)
    return is_max


def extract_keypoints(R, threshold_ratio=0.01, nms_window=7):
    """
    Extract keypoint locations from the Harris response map.
    
    Steps:
      1. Threshold: keep pixels where R > threshold_ratio * R.max()
      2. NMS: keep only local maxima of R
      3. Return (row, col) coordinates of detected corners
    """
    threshold = threshold_ratio * R.max()

    # Apply threshold
    above_thresh = R > threshold

    # Apply non-maximum suppression
    is_local_max = non_max_suppression_corners(R, window_size=nms_window)

    # Combine: corner = above threshold AND local maximum
    corners_mask = above_thresh & is_local_max

    # Get coordinates
    rows, cols = np.where(corners_mask)
    return rows, cols, corners_mask

Section D — Full Harris Detector Pipeline

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# D. COMPLETE HARRIS DETECTOR — from scratch
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def harris_detector(img, sigma_grad=1.0, sigma_window=1.5,
                     k=0.05, threshold_ratio=0.01, nms_window=7):
    """
    Full Harris corner detector from scratch.
    
    Parameters:
        img            : grayscale float [0,1]
        sigma_grad     : σ for pre-smoothing before gradient computation
        sigma_window   : σ for the Gaussian window w(x,y) in M
        k              : Harris sensitivity constant [0.04, 0.06]
        threshold_ratio: fraction of max(R) used as corner threshold
        nms_window     : NMS window size (avoids duplicate detections)
    Returns:
        keypoints : (rows, cols) arrays of detected corner coordinates
        R         : full corner response map
    """
    # Step 1-3: Compute structure matrix M
    M11, M12, M22, Ix, Iy = compute_structure_matrix(img, sigma_grad, sigma_window)

    # Step 4: Compute corner response R
    R = harris_response(M11, M12, M22, k)

    # Step 5: Extract keypoints via thresholding and NMS
    rows, cols, mask = extract_keypoints(R, threshold_ratio, nms_window)

    return (rows, cols), R


def visualise_harris(img, keypoints, R, max_points=500):
    """Visualise detected Harris corners on the image."""
    rows, cols = keypoints

    # Sort by R strength, keep top N
    strengths = R[rows, cols]
    order     = np.argsort(strengths)[::-1][:max_points]
    rows, cols = rows[order], cols[order]

    # Draw on image
    img_color = cv2.cvtColor((img * 255).astype(np.uint8), cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR)
    for r, c in zip(rows, cols):
        cv2.circle(img_color, (c, r), 4, (0, 255, 0), 1)
        cv2.circle(img_color, (c, r), 1, (0, 0, 255), -1)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))
    axes[0].imshow(img, cmap='gray');         axes[0].set_title('Original')
    axes[1].imshow(R, cmap='hot');            axes[1].set_title('Harris Response R')
    axes[2].imshow(img_color[..., ::-1]);     axes[2].set_title(f'Corners ({len(rows)} detected)')
    for ax in axes: ax.axis('off')
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Section E — Eigenvalue Analysis and Feature Matching 

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# E. EIGENVALUE ANALYSIS OF M
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def classify_pixels_by_eigenvalues(M11, M12, M22,
                                     thresh_corner=100,
                                     thresh_edge=10):
    """
    Classify every pixel as flat / edge / corner using eigenvalues of M.
    (Educational — Harris R score is the practical equivalent)
    
    M = [[M11, M12],
         [M12, M22]]
    
    Eigenvalues of 2x2 symmetric matrix:
        λ = (trace ± √(trace² - 4·det)) / 2
    """
    trace = M11 + M22                      # λ₁ + λ₂
    det   = M11 * M22 - M12**2            # λ₁ · λ₂
    disc  = np.sqrt(np.maximum(0, trace**2 / 4 - det))

    lam1 = trace / 2 + disc   # larger eigenvalue
    lam2 = trace / 2 - disc   # smaller eigenvalue

    # Classify based on eigenvalue magnitudes
    is_corner = (lam2 > thresh_corner)                           # both large
    is_edge   = (lam1 > thresh_edge) & (lam2 <= thresh_corner)  # only one large
    is_flat   = ~is_corner & ~is_edge                            # both small

    classification = np.full(M11.shape, 'flat', dtype=object)
    classification[is_edge]   = 'edge'
    classification[is_corner] = 'corner'

    return lam1, lam2, classification


# -----------------------------------------------------------
# F. FEATURE MATCHING USING HARRIS KEYPOINTS + SSD
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def extract_patch(img, row, col, half_size=8):
    """Extract a (2*half_size+1) × (2*half_size+1) patch centred at (row, col)."""
    r0, r1 = row - half_size, row + half_size + 1
    c0, c1 = col - half_size, col + half_size + 1
    if r0 < 0 or c0 < 0 or r1 > img.shape[0] or c1 > img.shape[1]:
        return None
    return img[r0:r1, c0:c1]


def match_keypoints_ssd(img1, img2, kp1, kp2, half_size=8, ratio_thresh=0.8):
    """
    Match keypoints between two images using SSD on raw patches.
    Applies Lowe's ratio test to filter ambiguous matches:
      accept match only if best_SSD < ratio_thresh * second_best_SSD.
    
    Returns list of (idx1, idx2, ssd_score) matched pairs.
    """
    rows1, cols1 = kp1
    rows2, cols2 = kp2
    matches = []

    for i, (r1, c1) in enumerate(zip(rows1, cols1)):
        patch1 = extract_patch(img1, r1, c1, half_size)
        if patch1 is None: continue

        distances = []
        for j, (r2, c2) in enumerate(zip(rows2, cols2)):
            patch2 = extract_patch(img2, r2, c2, half_size)
            if patch2 is None or patch2.shape != patch1.shape: continue
            distances.append((ssd(patch1, patch2), j))

        if len(distances) < 2: continue
        distances.sort()
        best_ssd, best_j   = distances[0]
        second_ssd, _      = distances[1]

        # Lowe's ratio test: accept only unambiguous matches
        if second_ssd > 0 and best_ssd / second_ssd < ratio_thresh:
            matches.append((i, best_j, best_ssd))

    return matches


# -----------------------------------------------------------
# G. USING OPENCV'S BUILT-IN HARRIS + FEATURE DETECTORS
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def harris_opencv(img_uint8, block_size=2, ksize=3, k=0.05):
    """
    OpenCV Harris detector.
    cv2.cornerHarris(img, blockSize, ksize, k)
      - blockSize: neighbourhood size for M computation (≈ window size)
      - ksize:     Sobel kernel size for gradient computation
      - k:         Harris sensitivity constant
    Returns the float32 R map. Threshold and visualise yourself.
    """
    img_f = img_uint8.astype(np.float32)
    R = cv2.cornerHarris(img_f, blockSize=block_size, ksize=ksize, k=k)
    # Normalise for display
    R_norm = cv2.normalize(R, None, 0, 255, cv2.NORM_MINMAX).astype(np.uint8)
    return R, R_norm


def full_demo(image_path):
    """Run everything on a real image."""
    img_uint8 = cv2.imread(image_path, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    img_float = img_uint8.astype(np.float32) / 255.0

    # Detect Harris corners
    keypoints, R = harris_detector(
        img_float,
        sigma_grad=1.0,
        sigma_window=1.5,
        k=0.05,
        threshold_ratio=0.01,
        nms_window=7
    )

    # Visualise
    visualise_harris(img_float, keypoints, R, max_points=300)

    # Compare with OpenCV
    R_cv2, _ = harris_opencv(img_uint8)
    print(f"Custom Harris found {len(keypoints[0])} corners")

    # Eigenvalue analysis
    M11, M12, M22, _, _ = compute_structure_matrix(img_float)
    lam1, lam2, classes  = classify_pixels_by_eigenvalues(M11, M12, M22)
    n_corners = np.sum(classes == 'corner')
    n_edges   = np.sum(classes == 'edge')
    print(f"Pixel classification: {n_corners} corners, {n_edges} edges")

# Quick synthetic test (no image file needed)
def quick_test():
    img = np.zeros((200, 200), dtype=np.float32)
    img[40:160, 40:160] = 1.0   # white square on black → 4 corners

    keypoints, R = harris_detector(img, threshold_ratio=0.02)
    rows, cols = keypoints
    print(f"Detected {len(rows)} corners at: {list(zip(rows.tolist(), cols.tolist()))}")

    plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
    plt.subplot(121); plt.imshow(img, cmap='gray')
    plt.plot(cols, rows, 'r+', ms=15, mew=2); plt.title('Detected Corners')
    plt.subplot(122); plt.imshow(R, cmap='hot'); plt.title('Harris Response R')
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

quick_test()
